did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens with a description of righteous leadership: the king is to reign justly, and the rulers are to act with justice.

Did you know? The role of a righteous leader is described through images of protection and well-being: a shelter from the wind, a refuge from the storm, streams of water in a dry land, and shade in a weary land.
Did you know? Alongside righteous leadership, the chapter describes spiritual and intellectual renewal: the eyes of those who see will no longer be closed, and the ears of those who hear will listen.
Did you know? The change also includes the ability to understand and speak: the hearts of the hasty will understand, and the tongues of those who stammer will speak clearly.
Did you know? Isaiah distinguishes between outward reputation and true character: the fool will no longer be called generous, nor the miser noble—that is, an important and generous person.
Did you know? The prophet describes the miser as someone who plans schemes to harm the poor, uses lies, and perverts the case of the needy.
Did you know? The complacent and confident women are called to wake up and listen, because their false sense of security is about to be shaken.

Did you know? The description of the destruction includes a drastic change in the landscape: the people’s land will be covered with thorns and briers, and the houses of joy and the joyful city will be abandoned.
Did you know? The turning point in the chapter comes when the Spirit is poured out from on high; afterward, the desert becomes fertile land, and the fertile land is considered a forest.
Did you know? Renewal involves not only a change in the landscape but also social restoration: justice will dwell in the desert, and righteousness will find its place in the fertile land.
Did you know? According to the chapter, the work of righteousness leads to peace, and its fruit is quietness and security forever.

Did you know? The chapter ends with a blessing for those who sow and work even under difficult conditions; the image of the ox and donkey emphasizes continued agricultural activity and prosperity near the water.
